strengths: The paper addresses a real and well-motivated bottleneck in Neural CDEs: the NFE of adaptive solvers is driven by the roughness of the interpolated control path. The core idea of replacing exact interpolation with kernel/GP smoothing to decouple integration cost from input noise is simple, sensible, and clearly articulated.

The theoretical framing (Theorem 3.1 relating NFE to the L1/(p+1)-quasi-norm of the (p+1)-th path derivative, Corollary 3.3 giving NFE ∝ h⁻¹, and Theorem 3.4 on the min-bandwidth bottleneck of block-diagonal parallel integration) provides useful design guidance and is consistent with the empirical solver-step and NFE observations.

The evaluation is thoughtfully designed: Pareto plots of error vs. training time, a solver-tolerance sweep on Linear/Cubic baselines to rule out the trivial 'just relax tolerance' counterargument, noise-robustness experiments confirming the NFE-vs-noise hypothesis, head-count/bandwidth ablations, and a computational cost breakdown separating one-time trajectory fitting from iterative training overhead.

The heteroscedastic attention-weighted GP path (Eq. 4), where attention scores modulate per-observation noise variance, is a neat mechanism connecting Q-Former-style querying to path construction, and the ablation (Table 1, Figures 7-9) shows the multi-view/attention component matters beyond plain GP smoothing.

The appendix (A.1-A.5, B, C) is substantive: proofs of the parallel-integration bottleneck, an explicit GP-vs-Nadaraya-Watson error comparison, full hyperparameters, and per-dataset optimization settings support reproducibility of the experimental claims.
weaknesses: The empirical scope is narrow relative to the claims. Only three UEA/UCR classification benchmarks are used, and — critically — all are regularly sampled (Appendix B.2 sets t ∈ {0,...,T}, ∆t = 1, with rectilinear padding). The paper motivates Neural CDEs by irregular sampling and missing data, but never evaluates on a genuinely irregularly sampled dataset. Claims of 'state-of-the-art accuracy' based on three datasets are overstated, especially since GRU-D achieves comparable accuracy at 2-5x lower wall-clock time on two of the three datasets.

Theorem 3.2 as stated is not rigorously established for the GP case. The claimed uniform bound sup‖d^p X_h/dt^p‖ ≤ C_p h^{-p} ‖X‖∞ holds cleanly for Nadaraya-Watson (weights sum to one), but the GP posterior mean coefficients (K+σ²I)⁻¹k(t) are not a normalized weight vector; their norm can grow as σ → 0, so the derivative bound cannot depend only on h and ‖X‖∞. The proof sketch ('linear operations on kernel functions... the bound follows immediately') glosses over this. Since Corollary 3.3 and the headline NFE ∝ h⁻¹ scaling build on Theorem 3.2, the theoretical chain has a gap.

Theorem 3.1's step from ‖d^{p+1}z/dt^{p+1}‖ ∝ ‖d^{p+1}X/dt^{p+1}‖ is heuristic: higher-order derivatives of z involve products and sums of derivatives of f_θ and X via the chain rule (Faà di Bruno terms), not simple linear scaling, even under Lipschitz boundedness. The theorem is labeled 'informal,' but the derived NFE estimates for splines (Eqs. 9, 11) are then presented as if exact.

There is an internal tension between the theory/motivation and the best configurations: Theorem 3.4 says NFE is governed by min h_m and Section 3.5/Appendix C.3 advocate multi-scale (heterogeneous) bandwidths, yet the best-performing main models (MVC GP in Table 1) use homogeneous, maximally large bandwidths (e.g., BW:[166.6,166.6,166.6,166.6]). This undercuts the 'spectrum of parameters to capture multi-scale dynamics' narrative.

The claim that attention 'recovers details lost during smoothing' / 'recovers high-frequency information' is not really supported by the method: the weighted GP path is still a low-pass construction whose bandwidths cap recoverable frequency content; attention only re-weights which observations are trusted. The mechanism mitigates over-smoothing but does not literally reconstruct lost high-frequency content, and no experiment directly measures reconstruction fidelity.

No code release or artifact link is mentioned, which limits reproducibility despite the detailed hyperparameter listings; the GP preprocessing is O(N³), and the paper's assertion that this overhead is 'negligible' is only demonstrated on sequences up to length 315, not on the long sequences where the method would matter most.

The speedup claims (4.3×-14.5×) are made only against CDE-family baselines; against the fastest accurate baseline (GRU-D) the method is slower on two of three datasets, which should be more prominently acknowledged in the abstract and contributions rather than only visible in Table 1.

strengths: The core observation — that adaptive-solver NFE in Neural CDEs is driven by the roughness of the interpolated control path, and that this can be decoupled from input noise via kernel/GP smoothing — is sensible, clearly motivated, and connects to known numerical analysis (LTE scaling with higher path derivatives).

The paper is generally well-organized: the pipeline (smoothing -> attention-weighted multi-scale paths -> block-diagonal parallel CDE integration) is described with sufficient implementation detail (Appendix B) that a practitioner could attempt to reimplement it.

The experiments include useful ablations: head-count sweeps (Fig. 6), bandwidth initialization (homogeneous vs. heterogeneous, Figs. 8-9), solver-tolerance analysis for spline baselines, a noise-robustness study (Fig. 4), and a computational cost breakdown (Fig. 10). Results are averaged over five seeds with error bars.
The noise-robustness experiment directly supports the mechanistic claim: NFE stays nearly constant under additive noise for smoothed paths while spline-based paths blow up.
Honest limitations are at least partially acknowledged, e.g., the parallel-integration bottleneck (Theorem 3.4) explicitly notes the cost is governed by the smallest bandwidth.
weaknesses: Overclaimed state of the art and efficiency. The claimed SOTA rests on only three small-to-medium UEA/UCR datasets, and the numbers do not clearly beat published results (e.g., SpokenArabicDigits and CharacterTrajectories accuracies of 98.3%/95.1% are below accuracies reported in the broader literature for these benchmarks). More importantly, Table 1 shows GRU-D is both substantially faster (2.02s vs 7.32s on SpokenArabicDigits; 10.56s vs 22.63s on CharacterTrajectories) and within ~2% accuracy of the proposed model, which contradicts the framing that smoothing-based CDEs make continuous-time models competitive with 'more traditional approaches' on efficiency.

The theoretical results are informal and partially circular. Theorem 3.1 is labeled 'informal' and reduces to proportionality statements; the chain-rule step asserting higher-order derivatives of z scale linearly with those of X assumes a bounded, Lipschitz vector field and ignores the feedback of z on the dynamics. Corollary 3.3's NFE ∝ h^{-1} and Theorem 3.4's bottleneck are plausible heuristics dressed as theorems. Appendix A.5's 'GPs provide the optimal linear reconstruction' is only optimal under the assumed GP prior — a tautology offered as justification for the cubic preprocessing cost.

The comparison is not apples-to-apples for the central speed claim. Showing that smoothed paths integrate faster than exact interpolants of the same noisy data is close to trivially expected; the more informative question is whether the smoothing + attention machinery beats simply smoothing the input (a preprocessing step) or relaxing solver tolerances, and the tolerance ablation (Figs. 7-9) shows the margin over spline baselines at relaxed tolerances is not dramatic.

Missing key baselines. The related work discusses Attentive NCDEs (Jhin et al., 2024), ContiFormer, Neural Rough DEs, and Structured Linear CDEs, but none are empirically compared. Given that Log-NCDE is the only modern efficiency baseline, the efficiency claims are established against a thin set.

The GP vs. kernel distinction is thin: with a shared RBF kernel, the GP posterior mean and Nadaraya-Watson estimator are near-identical linear smoothers (differing mainly through the noise term), yet the paper builds considerable narrative (and notation) around them as distinct contributions.

A causal-leakage issue is not discussed: the attention weights α_{m,k} are computed from the full sequence (via learnable queries over all observations), so path construction at time t depends on future observations. This undermines the streaming/causal advantages the paper attributes to CDE-style models and is a material caveat for the 'suitable for evolving input streams' framing.

Some reported configurations undercut the multi-scale story: the headline MVC GP models use identical bandwidths across heads (e.g., BW:[166.6,166.6,166.6,166.6]), so the advertised multi-view/multi-scale mechanism reduces to a heteroscedastic reweighting of a single scale in the main results; the heterogeneous initialization is relegated to appendix analysis.

Metrics are defined inconsistently: 'Average NFE per batch is reported... reflecting the numerical complexity of integrating the stiffest trajectory within a batch' conflates per-sample and per-batch quantities, making NFE comparisons across models with different M and batch sizes hard to interpret.
No code release is mentioned, and some hyperparameter notation in Table 1 (e.g., 'KS:3.0', bandwidth list semantics) is not fully defined, limiting reproducibility.

Novelty is moderate: smoothing for path construction has been examined (Morrill et al., 2022 on interpolation choices), and the attention component is an adaptation of Q-Former-style queries; the combination is reasonable engineering but the paper presents it with more generality than the three-dataset evidence supports.

strengths: The core idea is well-motivated and clearly articulated: adaptive solvers' NFE in Neural CDEs is governed by the roughness of the control path, so replacing exact interpolation with kernel/GP smoothing directly attacks the source of numerical stiffness. This is a genuinely different angle from prior work that regularizes latent dynamics (Kelly et al., Finlay et al.) or compresses the path algebraically (Log-NCDE, Neural Rough DEs).

The theoretical analysis, while informal, is coherent and useful: Theorem 3.1 links NFE to a quasi-norm of the (p+1)-th derivative of the control path, Theorem 3.2 gives bandwidth-controlled derivative bounds for Nadaraya-Watson/GP paths, and Theorem 3.4 correctly identifies the min-bandwidth bottleneck for parallel multi-head integration in block-diagonal systems. These results give the method a principled footing rather than being a pure heuristic.

The multi-view attentive recovery mechanism (MV-CDE/MVC-CDE) is a sensible and non-obvious design: it uses Q-Former-style learnable queries to re-inject high-frequency information lost by smoothing, and attention-derived weights are repurposed as heteroscedastic GP noise variances, which is an elegant coupling.

The empirical evaluation covers accuracy, NFE, wall-clock time, noise robustness (Figure 4), head-count/bandwidth ablations (Figure 6), Pareto frontiers under heterogeneous vs. homogeneous bandwidths, and a computational cost breakdown (Figure 10). The noise robustness experiment directly validates the central hypothesis: NFE stays nearly constant for smoothing methods while interpolants blow up.

Reproducibility is reasonably strong for an appendix-based paper: full hyperparameters per model and dataset (Table 1), preprocessing details, hardware, solver, seeds (5), and a fair-comparison protocol where Linear/Cubic baselines share the proposed methods' optimization schedule, plus tolerance sweeps showing spline baselines cannot be rescued by relaxing solver precision.
The limitations of the smoothing idea (information loss) are acknowledged and addressed within the method itself rather than hidden.
weaknesses: The empirical scope is narrow: only three UEA datasets, all with regular sampling (Δt = 1, rectilinear padding). Irregularly sampled time series are the motivating application of Neural CDEs, yet no experiment actually tests irregular timestamps, missing observations, or long sequences where the O(N^3) GP preprocessing cost could stop being 'negligible'. Claims of scalability are not stress-tested.

The 'state-of-the-art accuracy' claim is overreached given the baseline set. GRU-D achieves 96.57% on SpokenArabicDigits vs. 98.28% for MVC-GP while being 3.6x faster (2.02s vs. 7.32s), so the accuracy margin over a strong non-ODE baseline is modest on one of three datasets. More importantly, continuous-attention competitors discussed in the related work (ContiFormer, Attentive NCDE (Jhin et al. 2024), MANODE) are not compared empirically, which weakens the SOTA claim within the relevant model class.

There are internal inconsistencies between the theory/ablations and the actual best configurations. The multi-view story emphasizes a spectrum of bandwidths capturing multi-scale dynamics, but the primary models in Table 1 use uniform bandwidths (e.g., BW:[166.6,166.6,166.6,166.6] on CharacterTrajectories) with the lowest NFE — effectively collapsing to a single smooth path. Meanwhile Appendix C.3 argues heterogeneous initialization is superior, yet the main results use homogeneous settings. The role of multi-head attention in the final system is therefore less clear than the narrative suggests.

The theory is informal and relies on heuristic steps presented as theorems. In particular, the claim that higher-order derivatives of z(t) scale linearly with those of X(t) assumes fθ is Lipschitz and bounded, but the vector field is a learned neural network whose higher-order behavior is uncontrolled; the 'NFE ∝ h^{-1}' result is a first-order scaling argument whose constants and regime of validity are not examined.

Theorem 3.4 (parallel bottleneck) implies that adding heads with small bandwidths should dominate total NFE, yet Table 1 shows MV/MVC variants often have NFE comparable to or higher than single-path smoothing for reasons the theory does not explain (e.g., MV GP on UWave: 359 vs. GP's 170.6). The mismatch between the predicted (min h)^{-1} scaling and observed per-head costs deserves analysis.

The noise robustness test injects noise only at test time with fixed hyperparameters; a more convincing evaluation would also consider training-time noise or hyperparameter re-selection, and report whether the GP lengthscale h chosen on clean data remains appropriate under heavy perturbation.

Some presentation issues reduce clarity: the main results table (Table 1) is relegated to the appendix, several Pareto plots (Figures 3, 7–9) are cluttered and hard to read, and the contribution list in the introduction is inflated (five bullets where three would suffice, with 'temporal parallelization' framing repeated without added substance).

strengths: The paper addresses a real and well-motivated bottleneck: the computational cost (NFE) of adaptive-solver Neural CDEs driven by rough interpolated control paths. The idea of decoupling integration cost from input noise via kernel/GP smoothing, then recovering detail with a Q-Former-inspired multi-view attention mechanism, is sensible and clearly articulated.

The theoretical framing is a genuine strength: Theorem 3.1 connects NFE to a quasi-norm of the (p+1)-th derivative of the control path, and the appendix derives explicit NFE scalings for linear/cubic interpolants versus smoothed paths (Corollary 3.3) and a multi-head bottleneck result (Theorem 3.4) that matches the empirical 'stiffest head' phenomenon. The GP vs. Nadaraya-Watson error comparison (A.5) gives a clean justification for preferring GP smoothing at fixed bandwidth.

The experimental section is unusually thorough for this problem: capacity-matched baselines, solver-tolerance sweeps showing baselines cannot be trivially accelerated, noise-robustness curves with NFE tracking, head-count ablations, bandwidth initialization ablations, solver-order analysis, high-dimensional scalability (PEMS-SF, 963 dims), memory comparisons against Mamba, and a smoothing-spline baseline to rule out the trivial 'just smooth the data' explanation.

The limitations section is honest and substantive (solver dependency, bandwidth sensitivity, stiffest-head bottleneck, high-frequency information loss), and the treatment of causal/offline smoothing in streaming forecasting is handled carefully with reference to Morrill et al. (2022).
weaknesses: The 'state-of-the-art accuracy' claim in the abstract and conclusion is overclaimed. On CharacterTrajectories, Mamba (96.64%) outperforms the best proposed model MVC GP (95.07%), and GRU-D trains ~3.5x faster than MVC GP on SpokenArabicDigits. The method is best described as competitive on accuracy with strong efficiency over spline CDEs, not uniformly SOTA.

The theory is heuristic in places. The proof of Theorem 3.2 glosses over the fact that the Nadaraya-Watson estimator has t-dependent normalization weights whose derivatives also scale with h, so the stated bound on the derivative of X_h(t) does not follow immediately from the kernel derivative bound. Similarly, the chain-rule step ||z^{(p+1)}|| ∝ ||X^{(p+1)}|| in A.1 is asserted without proof under only Lipschitz/boundedness of f_theta, and the NFE bound is stated as an asymptotic proportionality rather than a rigorous result. This weakens the theoretical contribution's precision.

There is a gap between theory and the actual method: Theorem 3.2, Corollary 3.3, and the GP optimality argument in A.5 assume fixed kernels, fixed bandwidths, and fixed noise. In the actual model, attention weights alpha_{m,k} are learned and input-dependent, and the heteroscedastic noise Sigma_m in Eq. (4) depends on the model parameters. The claimed derivative bounds and strict GP optimality therefore do not directly apply to the deployed MV/MVC paths, and no discussion is given of gradients flowing through the (K_h + Sigma_m)^{-1} solve during training.

Evaluation breadth is limited: the main claims rest on only three UEA datasets, with supplementary datasets used for specific robustness/scalability probes. Given the breadth of the UEA archive and the explicit comparison to recent attention-based CDE variants (Attentive NCDEs, ContiFormer) that are cited but not benchmarked, the empirical case for generality is thinner than the framing suggests.

Some efficiency claims require careful qualification: the multi-view mechanism shares the block-diagonal structure of Structured Linear CDEs, part of the accuracy gain is attributable to the convolutional front-end rather than smoothing per se (per the component-wise decomposition), and the headline speedups (5x-14x) are against spline CDEs whose NFEs are inflated by noise—the paper does demonstrate the tolerance-sweep control, but the practical speedup versus well-tuned discrete baselines is far smaller.

No explicit code release or reproducibility statement is included, which is a concern given the many dataset-specific hyperparameter choices (bandwidth grids, per-dataset tolerances, capacity matching) needed to reproduce the results.

strengths: The paper addresses a real and well-motivated problem: the sensitivity of adaptive-solver NFE to the roughness of the interpolated control path in Neural CDEs, and the geometric framing (decoupling integration cost from input noise) is clear and coherent.

The experimental protocol is unusually thorough: capacity-matched baselines, five random seeds, Pareto plots of accuracy vs. wall-clock time, noise-injection robustness sweeps, solver-order ablations (bosh3/dopri5/dopri8), a smoothing-spline control baseline, irregular-sampling tests (Speech Commands at 30%/50% drops), high-dimensional scalability (PEMS-SF, 963-dim), and memory profiling (Table 3). This goes well beyond a typical benchmark table.

The ablation structure (single-path kernel/GP → +attention → +convolution) reasonably isolates the source of the reported gains, e.g., cubic NFE ≈ 1042 vs. GP ≈ 171 on UWave, with the multi-view/convolution components adding accuracy on top.

The limitations section is candid and specific (solver dependency, bandwidth tuning, stiffest-head bottleneck, loss of frequency information), and the causality/offline-smoothing caveat is honestly discussed rather than hidden.
weaknesses: The theory does not actually cover the proposed method. Theorem 3.2's derivative bound is argued for a stationary RBF kernel and uniform data, but the core contribution—Eq. (4), the heteroscedastic attention-weighted GP path where Σm depends on learned attention scores—is outside these assumptions, and no NFE or regularity bound is established for the weighted paths. The 'proof' that ∥d^{p+1}z/dt^{p+1}∥ ∝ ∥d^{p+1}X/dt^{p+1}∥ (Appendix A.1) is hand-wavy: the chain rule for high-order derivatives of the driven state involves products and nested derivatives of fθ, which are neither Lipschitz-bounded nor analyzed. The 'strictly determined' language in Theorem 3.1 overstates what is an upper bound under unstated assumptions. Theorem 3.4 is essentially the trivial observation that a block-diagonal ODE is constrained by its stiffest component.

The central idea has limited originality. Replacing exact interpolation with kernel or GP smoothing is a classical preprocessing operation, and GP-based smoothing/adaptation for irregular time series is well documented (the paper itself cites Li & Marlin 2016, Futoma et al. 2017, Shukla & Marlin 2019/2020); the delta over prior work reduces to an attention-weighted multi-scale version of this smoother plus a block-diagonal CDE integration, both incremental. The 'temporal parallelization' framing is marketing more than a technical mechanism, since the ODE is still solved sequentially.

The headline 'state-of-the-art accuracy' claim is only partially supported. On CharacterTrajectories, Mamba (96.64%) clearly outperforms the proposed MVC GP (95.07%), so the method is SOTA on 2 of 3 main benchmarks at best; GRU-D is also substantially faster (10.6s vs. 22.6s) on CharacterTrajectories and 2.0s vs. 7.3s on SpokenArabicDigits, which softens the efficiency narrative versus discrete baselines.

Evidence of inconsistency in the multi-scale story: the appendix analysis praises heterogeneous bandwidth initialization (Figure 8), yet the best main-result configurations use homogeneous, maximal bandwidths (BW:[166.6,166.6,166.6,166.6] on CharacterTrajectories; [91,91,91] on SpokenArabicDigits), undermining the 'multi-view recovers diverse temporal scales' motivation for the architecture. Similarly, the abstract claims 5×–14× speedups while Section 4.3 reports 4.3×–14.5×.

Main-text evaluation rests on only three UEA datasets; the broader evidence (PEMS-SF, Speech Commands, ETTm1) is confined to the appendix, and the ETTm1 forecasting result compares against only GRU and Cubic NCDE—no modern forecasting baselines (DLinear itself, PatchTST, etc.), so the forecasting claim is weakly anchored.

The heteroscedastic noise construction σ²_base/(α_{m,k}+ε) is an ad hoc heuristic with no analysis of how softmax-bounded attention scores (α ≤ 1) translate into meaningful noise-variance modulation; the claimed connection to 'optimal parameter estimation properties of GPs' (Zaytsev & Burnaev, 2014) does not substantiate this design choice.

Reproducibility concerns: no code release is mentioned; the tuning asymmetry is acknowledged but hard to audit (bandwidth sweep over [0.01, 9.0] for proposed methods vs. separately optimized learning rates/tolerances for baselines), and several key details (e.g., how bandwidth interacts with padding, the exact attention parameterization dimension d_ctx) are scattered across the appendix.

strengths: The paper targets a real and well-recognized bottleneck of Neural CDEs (NFE growth driven by rough/noisy control paths) and the core idea—decoupling integration cost from input noise via kernel/GP smoothing—is sensible and clearly articulated.

The theoretical framing is useful: relating NFE to a quasi-norm of the (p+1)-th path derivative (Thm 3.1) and showing NFE scales as δ^{-1/(p+1)} h^{-1} for smoothed paths (Cor. 3.3), plus the multi-head bottleneck analysis (Thm 3.4), gives practitioners concrete guidance on the bandwidth/efficiency trade-off.

The experimental methodology is largely careful: capacity-matched baselines (Table 3), multiple solver tolerance points for spline baselines to rule out trivial tolerance-relaxation speedups, noise robustness sweeps, solver-order ablations, irregular-sampling tests, and an honest, specific limitations section (bandwidth sensitivity, stiffest-head bottleneck, solver dependency).

The ablations (head count, heterogeneous vs. homogeneous bandwidths, head diversity regularization) genuinely probe the design choices, and the component-wise decomposition (Table 2) shows each piece (smoothing, attention, convolution) contributes measurably.
Supplementary results (Speech Commands with 30/50% drops, PEMS-SF with 963 dimensions, ETTm1 forecasting) go beyond the three main UEA datasets and strengthen the empirical case.
weaknesses: The claim of 'state-of-the-art accuracy' is overstated: the main comparison covers only three UEA datasets, and on CharacterTrajectories Mamba (96.64%) actually outperforms the proposed MVC GP (95.07%). A broader benchmark suite (the UEA archive has ~30 datasets) would be needed to support the SOTA claim.

The central theory is looser than presented. Theorem 3.1's step from LTE bounds on z(t) to the (p+1)-th derivative of X(t) relies on the heuristic proportionality ‖z^{(p+1)}‖ ∝ ‖X^{(p+1)}‖; the chain rule through a general Lipschitz vector field fθ does not give this cleanly, since z^{(p+1)} mixes derivatives of fθ and all lower-order derivatives of X. Theorem 3.2's bound in terms of ‖X‖∞ (rather than a smoothness norm of the latent signal) is quite loose. The results are plausible heuristics but are stated as theorems without the needed rigor.

There is an apparent inconsistency in the efficiency accounting: the paper claims GP smoothing is a 'static, one-time preprocessing cost,' but in the MV/MVC models the attention weights α_{m,k} (and hence the heteroscedastic noise Σ_m and the GP solve (K_h + Σ_m)^{-1}X) depend on learnable parameters and must be recomputed each forward pass during training. The claimed O(N³) one-time-cost argument strictly applies only to the single-path, non-attention models; the paper should clarify how per-iteration refitting is handled and whether the reported overheads account for it.

Terminology conflation: the paper repeatedly attributes the effect to 'stiffness,' but the mechanism described is path roughness/jaggedness forcing small adaptive steps. ODE stiffness has a distinct technical meaning (eigenvalues of the Jacobian of the vector field); the analysis and language should be more precise.

Some efficiency comparisons are less favorable than the headline claims suggest: GRU-D and Mamba are substantially faster in wall-clock time on several datasets (e.g., GRU-D 2–10s vs. MVC GP 7–23s), so the speedup claims apply specifically relative to spline-based CDEs, and the paper should be clearer that the contribution is within the CDE family rather than against all sequence models.

The design of attention-weighted heteroscedastic noise (variance inversely proportional to attention score) is heuristic and end-to-end learned without theoretical justification; the ablation showing that explicitly enforcing head diversity hurts accuracy suggests the attention mechanism's role is not fully understood.

No code release or reproducibility artifact is mentioned, despite heavy reliance on specific hyperparameter sweeps (bandwidth grids, tolerance settings, per-dataset schedules) that would be difficult to reconstruct exactly.
